extracted.intended_audience: general public, voters, and researchers looking for a summary of the event
extracted.subtask_short: encyclopedic article on a senate resignation
extracted.subtask_description: A Ballotpedia encyclopedic summary of Al Franken's 2017–2018 sexual misconduct allegations, the political responses calling for his resignation, and the Minnesota procedures used to fill his U.S. Senate seat. Covers timeline of allegations, statements from senators, appointment and special-election mechanics, and related links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minnesota procedure for filling a U.S. Senate vacancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Minnesota law lays out the procedures for filling vacancies in the United States Senate: after the vacancy occurred, Gov. Mark Dayton (D) appointed Lieutenant Gov. Tina Smith (D) to fill the seat until the next regularly scheduled general election on November 6, 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breakdown provided: the governor appoints a temporary replacement who serves until the next regularly scheduled general election; a special primary to select partisan candidates (held August 14, 2018) preceded the November special election; the winner served until Franken's original term expired (January 3, 2021). If a resignation occurs less than 11 weeks before a regularly scheduled primary, the appointee would not face an election until the following year (example dates: May 29, 2018 was the date 11 weeks before the August 14 primary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment authority and timing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The governor may appoint a replacement (here, Tina Smith) and timing of a resignation can affect when an appointee must face election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the page: Franken announced his resignation would take effect on January 2, 2018, allowing Smith to be sworn into office on January 3. The page explains the strategic/timing implication: had Franken resigned less than 11 weeks before a scheduled primary, Smith would not have faced an election until the following year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and chronology of allegations used as grounds for calls to resign
rubrics_metrics.description: The article catalogs allegations against Franken (forcible kiss during a 2006 USO tour, photo showing hands on/near a woman's chest while she slept, groping incidents at a state fair, photo-op and fundraiser incidents, alleged groping in Kuwait in 2003, and an alleged wet open-mouthed kiss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents a timeline with dates and sources (e.g., Leeann Tweeden Nov 16, 2017; Lindsay Menz Nov 20, 2017; additional anonymous accounts Nov 22, 2017; Stephanie Kemplin Nov 30, 2017). It notes the presence of photographic evidence in at least one allegation and includes Franken's various responses (apology, denial, calls for ethics investigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and rationales cited by Democratic senators calling for resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous Democratic senators publicly stated reasons for asking Franken to resign, citing obligations to constituents and the Senate and asserting that sexual harassment and misconduct are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and rationales include: 'Senator Franken should resign. I consider Senator Franken a dear friend and greatly respect his accomplishments, but he has a higher obligation to his constituents and the Senate, and he should step down immediately.'; 'It’s time for us as elected representatives to hold ourselves to a higher standard'; 'Sexual harassment and misconduct are never acceptable.' The page reports that as of Dec. 6, 35 of 48 members of the Democratic Caucus had called for his resignation (including 13 of 16 women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate between immediate resignation versus awaiting an Ethics Committee process
rubrics_metrics.description: Some officials and commentators emphasized immediate resignation while others emphasized the role of the Senate Ethics Committee and due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: Franken urged the Senate to open an ethics investigation; both Senate leaders (Mitch McConnell and Chuck Schumer) called for an investigation; Kirsten Gillibrand said 'While Senator Franken is entitled to have the Ethics Committee conclude its review, I believe it would be better... if he sent a clear message... by stepping aside'; later reporting showed some senators regretted the push for resignation and questioned whether due process was adequately observed (Politico reported senators like Joe Manchin and Patrick Leahy expressing regret).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political consequences and intra-party dynamics as factors in response
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents how political calculations and intra-party reactions shaped responses—initial unified calls, followed by later expressions of regret or criticism of how the situation was handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/examples: Politico reported that some senators who had called for resignation later regretted it and criticized the Democrats' handling ('What they did to Al was atrocious... The most hypocritical thing I’ve ever seen done to a human being' — Joe Manchin). The page notes which senators changed or maintained positions (e.g., Gillibrand did not change her position; Schumer reportedly did not change his mind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public response and remedial actions by the accused
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses by Franken included apologies, denial of some allegations, and calls for an ethics investigation; these public steps formed part of the narrative about how to address allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: Franken said 'I certainly don’t remember the rehearsal for the skit in the same way, but I send my sincerest apologies...' and 'I can categorically say that I did not proposition anyone...' He urged the Senate to open an ethics investigation and at times cooperated via spokesperson statements. The page frames apology, cooperation with investigation, and public statements as components of the accused's response strategy.
